abstract: Research examining geographic variation in AI vulnerability across US metropolitan areas, finding that high-education metros are the most exposed to AI-driven labor market disruption. Unlike previous automation waves that primarily affected manufacturing-heavy regions, AI's impact concentrates in knowledge-economy metros with large shares of professional, analytical, and administrative workers whose tasks overlap significantly with generative AI capabilities.
keyFindings: High-education metropolitan areas are the most vulnerable to AI-driven labor disruption
AI exposure patterns differ sharply from previous automation waves that hit manufacturing regions
Knowledge-economy metros with large professional workforces face the greatest task-level AI overlap
Geographic concentration of AI-exposed occupations creates regional economic risk
methodology: Geographic analysis mapping AI task exposure scores to US metropolitan area employment composition, comparing AI vulnerability patterns to historical automation exposure distributions.
qualifiers: Exposure does not equal displacement; high-education metros may also be better positioned to adapt. Metropolitan-level analysis masks within-metro variation by neighborhood and demographic group. Task exposure metrics are model-based estimates with inherent uncertainty.
